title: China Overtakes U.S. in Global Popularity, but India Remains a Rare Pro-American Holdout
excerpt: A Pew Research Center survey of 36 countries finds China is now viewed more favorably than the United States for the first time in two decades — but India, alongside just five other nations, still backs Washington.
body:
• In 25 of 36 countries surveyed by Pew Research Center, more people now view China favorably than the U.S. — the first such reversal in roughly 20 years of tracking.
  • India is one of only six nations — alongside Japan, South Korea, the Philippines, Poland, and Israel — where the U.S. still holds a favorability edge over China.
  • A separate Gallup poll of 130+ countries found China's leadership approval at 36% versus 31% for the U.S. in 2025, the widest gap in China's favor in nearly two decades.

China has overtaken the United States in global public opinion for the first time in two decades, according to a sweeping Pew Research Center survey published on July 15. But India — home to 1.4 billion people and one of Washington's most significant strategic partners — remains firmly in America's corner, keeping the superpower contest from becoming a rout.

The survey, which interviewed 42,151 adults across 36 countries between February and May 2026, found that more people hold favorable views of China than of the U.S. in 25 of those nations. Only six countries — India, Japan, the Philippines, South Korea, Poland, and Israel — still rate the U.S. more positively than China.

A Dramatic Reversal

The shift is both recent and rapid. In 2023, the U.S. held a clear favorability lead over China in most countries Pew surveyed. That advantage has since evaporated, driven by a simultaneous decline in America's image and a steady rise in China's standing.

Canada illustrates the scale of the change. Just three years ago, 57% of Canadians viewed the U.S. favorably while only 14% held positive views of China. By 2026, those numbers had flipped: 44% now view China favorably, compared with 33% for the U.S. — a 30-point swing in each direction, according to Pew.

A separate Gallup survey of more than 130 countries, based on 2025 data, reinforced the trend. It found median global approval of China's leadership at 36%, compared with 31% for the U.S. — the widest margin in China's favor that Gallup has recorded in nearly 20 years. U.S. leadership disapproval hit a record-high 48%.

"The soft-power gap the U.S. long took for granted has narrowed to the point of reversal — and this reversal is broad-based, not concentrated in any single region or bloc."

— The Brief, analyzing the Pew findings

Why India Stands Apart

India's position as a pro-American holdout is shaped by geography, security, and direct experience with Chinese power. New Delhi manages an active border dispute with Beijing along the Line of Actual Control, where deadly clashes in 2020 marked the worst military confrontation between the two countries in decades.

The other five countries that still favor the U.S. share a similar thread. Japan, South Korea, and the Philippines operate under U.S. security alliances in the Indo-Pacific. Poland sits on NATO's eastern flank bordering Russia. Israel's defense relationship with Washington is foundational. The pattern suggests that proximity to a security threat — and dependence on American strategic commitments — is the variable most resistant to the broader erosion in U.S. standing.

On leadership ratings, the story is similar. Chinese President Xi Jinping now outpolls U.S. President Donald Trump in 22 of 36 countries, including traditional American allies like Canada, Mexico, France, Germany, and the United Kingdom. But in India, Japan, and the Philippines — nations that share borders or territorial tensions with China — Trump still receives higher confidence ratings than Xi.

The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian diaspora, the findings carry a dual significance. Indians abroad often navigate between two superpowers competing for influence in their countries of residence. In nations across Europe, Latin America, and Southeast Asia — where China's image has surged — public sentiment is shifting in ways that may reshape trade flows, diplomatic alignments, and the broader environment in which diaspora communities operate. India's own pro-American tilt, meanwhile, underscores how border tensions with China continue to anchor New Delhi's strategic orientation, even as much of the world recalibrates.

What's Next

The Pew survey closed on May 13, one day before Xi and Trump met in Beijing on May 14 — meaning the data does not capture any potential shift from that summit. As Washington and Beijing jockey for influence through tariffs, technology restrictions, and infrastructure investment in the Global South, the next round of polling will test whether the reversal is a structural realignment or a snapshot driven by the current political cycle.

Gallup's analysts offered a cautious framing, noting that 45% of countries surveyed in 2025 delivered negative net approval ratings to both the U.S. and China. The contest, in other words, may be less about which superpower is winning hearts than about which is losing them more slowly.
nri_angle: India is one of only six countries that still views the U.S. more favorably than China, a position shaped by border tensions with Beijing that directly affects how the diaspora navigates great-power competition abroad.
author: Diaspora Desk
